analysis.one_liner: Bans bankruptcy courts from wiping out lawsuits against companies that never filed for bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: In recent years, large corporations facing thousands of injury and liability lawsuits have filed for bankruptcy and persuaded the court to also wipe out — or permanently block — claims against related companies, like a parent or sister company, that never went bankrupt themselves. This bill would amend federal bankruptcy law to stop courts from releasing or enjoining the liability of any company other than the one that actually filed for bankruptcy, except with that company's clear, written consent. It would also cap temporary shields against lawsuits at 90 days, let claimants immediately appeal such shields, and let courts dismiss bankruptcy cases where a company deliberately split its assets from its liabilities before filing.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people with legal claims against large companies — injury victims, asbestos and product-liability claimants, workers, and consumers — would keep their right to sue the companies actually responsible, even after one part of a corporate family files for bankruptcy. Creditors who might otherwise be shortchanged by a corporate restructuring designed to park liabilities in a shell would also gain a stronger remedy, since courts could dismiss cases involving such asset-liability splits.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits bankruptcy courts from discharging or releasing the legal liability of a company that did not file for bankruptcy, so people injured or owed money can keep suing the responsible parties.
It limits temporary injunctions shielding non-bankrupt companies from lawsuits to 90 days unless the claimant expressly consents, ending indefinite legal protection.
It gives claimants an immediate right to appeal any order temporarily staying their lawsuit during a bankruptcy.

It lets courts dismiss a bankruptcy case where the debtor was created or restructured in the previous ten years to separate its assets from its liabilities — the so-called 'Texas two-step' tactic — so a company cannot bury its debts in a hollowed-out shell.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their affiliates facing mass liability claims would lose a tool they have increasingly used to end lawsuits through bankruptcy: the nondebtor release and the third-party injunction. Companies that have carried out asset-liability splits in the previous ten years would face a new risk that a bankruptcy court dismisses their case.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the current practice argue that some reorganizations are only possible if a bankrupt company can bring along related companies — often a parent or affiliate that agreed to the structure — in a global settlement, and that a hard ban could make some large bankruptcies harder to resolve and reduce the money available to creditors.

The bill restricts courts' flexibility: it bars even a voluntarily negotiated release unless the affected claimant gives express written consent after clear notice, which could slow down settlements that all parties would otherwise accept.

The proposed 'Texas two-step' dismissal rule requires a showing of intent or foreseeable effect of splitting assets from liabilities within the prior ten years, which could pull courts into contested factual disputes about ordinary corporate restructurings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is significant: lawsuits — from asbestos claims to product liability and wage claims — would again be decided against the actual wrongdoers, not erased by a bankruptcy court's order shielding companies that never filed for bankruptcy. The main cost acknowledged by critics of the ban is that some genuinely complicated reorganizations, where a parent company's cooperation is needed to fund a settlement, could become harder to close, potentially reducing recovery for some claimants and raising financing costs for distressed companies. The bill tries to soften this with a 90-day limit on temporary stays, an express-consent exception, and a carve-out for corporate divisions done without intent to shed liabilities, but the core change would end a practice that has become routine in large bankruptcies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Jerrold Nadler introduced the Nondebtor Release Prohibition Act on July 30, 2024.
It was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, where it stayed with no markup, no vote, and no floor action.

The bill was a response to the growing use of bankruptcy by large corporations to get court orders releasing related companies — including parents that never went bankrupt — from legal liability to people harmed by their products.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired without any action beyond referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use the bankruptcy system to escape liability to injured people and other creditors kept the existing rules intact, since no restriction on nondebtor releases was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that escape lawsuits via bankruptcy courts

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 30, 2024 to ban nonconsensual nondebtor releases in bankruptcy.

for.name: Reps. Steve Cohen (D-TN), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-DC), Katie Porter (D-CA), Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA), and Hank Johnson (D-GA)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by six House Democrats and never reached a vote, so no roll-call revealed whether Republicans or additional Democrats would have supported it.

industries.industry: Major corporations facing mass-tort and product liability claims (chemical, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, and their parent companies)
industries.note: The bill would end the practice of using bankruptcy to obtain court orders wiping out or enjoining lawsuits against non-bankrupt affiliates and parents, leaving them exposed to the full amount of legal claims. This is the concentrated interest that lobbies for the current system's preservation.

The bill narrows the tools restructuring lawyers and financial advisers can offer clients, particularly the 'Texas two-step' divisional merger strategy, reducing demand for this style of high-fee bankruptcy work.

Restrictions on nondebtor releases and stays change the expected recovery and risk profile of loans to corporate groups, and some financing that relies on bankruptcy protections could become more expensive or less available.
